title: Using cameras to index waterfowl abundance in winter-flooded rice fields
author: Firth, Baker, et al.
materials: LEISA non-flooded (LN; long-term non-flooded, no till), (

steps.title: Select sites and treatment fields
steps.instruction: Choose two rice‑production sites (a Low‑external‑input‑sustainable agriculture (LEISA) site and a conventional site) and assign each field to one of four treatment regimes: LEISA flooded (LF), LEISA non‑flooded (LN), conventional flooded (CF), or conventional non‑flooded (CN). Each field used for camera surveys must be approximately 40 ha in size.

steps.title: Install cameras and reference stakes
steps.instruction: In each 40 ha field install three no‑glow infrared camera traps (Stealth Cam® G42NG): one along the southern field edge and two in the northern corners facing southeast and southwest. Place a metal stake 30.4 m directly in front of each camera to serve as a distance reference; this defines a sampling area of 242.32 m² (reported elsewhere as 242.232 m²) directly in front of each camera.

steps.title: Program and maintain camera traps
steps.instruction: Program each camera to capture one picture every hour from 3 Nov 2017 through 15 Mar 2018. Retrieve and replace the memory cards on a monthly schedule. Record any camera loss: theft of 3 cameras in Jan 2018, failure of 2 cameras in Dec 2017, and obstruction (fallen over) of 2 cameras in Jan 2018, which will create gaps in the image record.

steps.title: Download images and set up analysis layer
steps.instruction: Download all images from each camera’s memory card. Open the images in GNU Image Manipulation Program (GIMP). Create an image layer that outlines the 242.32 m² sampling area using the 30.4 m reference stake as a guide. Overlay this layer on every discernible photo before counting.

steps.title: Count waterfowl in each image
steps.instruction: For each hourly photo, count all waterfowl (geese and ducks) within the defined area; mark each bird with a red dot to avoid recounting. Exclude non‑waterfowl birds (they represent <10 % of observations).

steps.title: Validate counts with double‑observer test
steps.instruction: After the lead researcher has logged species and abundances for all photographs, randomly select 30 photographs. Have the lead researcher and a second observer independently recount those 30 images. Compare the two sets of counts with a one‑way ANOVA (result reported: F₂,₈₇ = 0.001, P = 0.999) to confirm no observer bias.

steps.title: Calculate daily and seasonal densities
steps.instruction:
Perform the following five calculations for each field:
1) Count geese and ducks separately in the 242.32 m² area and average the counts for each 24‑h day that has pictures.
2) Compute the average number of geese and ducks per day per m².
3) Convert the per‑m² values to per‑ha values (multiply by 10,000 m²/ha).
4) Average the per‑ha values among the three cameras within the same field to obtain geese‑or‑duck / day / ha for that field.
5) Average these field‑level values across the entire season, weighting by the number of active camera days for each field, to obtain the seasonal waterfowl / day / ha used for downstream fecal‑input estimates.
